text: When all the Amorite kings west of the Jordan and all the Canaanite kings along the sea heard how the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the Israelites until they had crossed over, their hearts melted, and no courage was left in any of them because of the Israelites.
At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make yourself flint knives and circumcise the Israelites again."
So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the Israelites at Gibeath-haaraloth.^[Gibeath-haaraloth means "the hill of the foreskins."]

versions.text: So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the Israelites at Gibeath-haaraloth.
versions.explanation: The place name is meaningful in Hebrew and explains the naming of the site; a brief footnote helps the listener or reader understand why this name is given here.

text: This was the reason Joshua circumcised them: all the males who came out of Egypt, all the fighting men, had died in the wilderness along the way after they left Egypt.
All the people who came out had been circumcised, but none of those born in the wilderness along the way after they left Egypt had been circumcised.

The Israelites had walked forty years in the wilderness until the whole nation—the fighting men who came out of Egypt—had perished, because they had not obeyed the voice of the LORD. To them the LORD had sworn that they would never see the land he had promised on oath to their fathers to give us, a land flowing with milk and honey.
So he raised up their sons in their place, and these were the ones Joshua circumcised. They were still uncircumcised, since they had not been circumcised along the way.
When the whole nation had been circumcised, they stayed where they were in the camp until they had healed.
Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the disgrace of Egypt from you." So that place has been called Gilgal to this day.
While the Israelites were camped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, on the plains of Jericho.
The day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate the produce of the land: unleavened bread and roasted grain.
The manna stopped the day after they ate the produce of the land. The Israelites had no more manna, but ate the crops of the land of Canaan that year.
Now while Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in his hand. Joshua went up to him and asked, "Are you for us or for our enemies?"
"Neither," he replied. "I am the commander of the LORD's army. Now I have come." Then Joshua fell facedown to the ground in worship and said to him, "What does my lord have to say to his servant?"

versions.text: "Neither," he replied. "I have come as commander of the army of the LORD." Then Joshua fell facedown to the ground in worship and said to him, "What does my Lord have to say to his servant?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew contains two distinct statements: an identification ("I am the commander of the LORD's army") and an announcement of arrival ("now I have come"). Collapsing them into "I have come as commander" loses the emphatic self-identification and the temporal "now," which carries the sense that his appearing is a decisive moment.

versions.text: "Neither," he replied. "I am the commander of the LORD's army. Now I have come." Then Joshua fell facedown to the ground in worship and said to him, "What does my Lord have to say to his servant?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew here is אֲדֹנִי (adoni), the ordinary respectful address to a superior, not the divine title. Capitalizing "Lord" resolves an ambiguity the narrative deliberately leaves open at this point and can be confused with the small-caps LORD used for the divine name earlier in the same verse. Lowercase "my lord" keeps Joshua's deferential address without prejudging the figure's identity.

text: The commander of the LORD's army answered, "Take off your sandal from your foot, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.

versions.text: The commander of the LORD's army answered, "Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is singular ("your sandal from your foot"), distinguishing this command from the plural form in Exodus 3:5. Including "from your foot" also preserves the fuller rhythm of the Hebrew phrase for oral reading.
